summary.text: La Niña is the cooling phase of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the colder counterpart of El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean.
La Niña events cause short-term cooling of global surface temperature, and together with El Niño they can bring intense storms in some places and droughts in others.
It matches the positive phase of the Southern Oscillation, when Pacific air pressure takes the opposite pattern to the one seen during El Niño.

facts.label: Older names
facts.value: Anti-El Niño and El Viejo, 'the old man'

facts.label: How often
facts.value: Part of a cycle of roughly two to seven years

items.prompt: A strong La Niña sets in. What would you expect global average surface temperature to do for a while?

options.label: Spike up briefly
Stay perfectly flat
Dip briefly
Fall for good

items.explain: La Niña events cause short-term cooling of the surface, the reverse of El Niño's short warm spikes.

items.prompt: Over a ten-year stretch, La Niña events happen far more often than El Niño events. How could that shape the global temperature trend for that decade?

options.label: It could hold the trend lower
It could push the trend higher
It has no effect over ten years
It would end warming for good

items.explain: Because La Niña cools and El Niño warms the surface, their relative frequency can affect global temperature trends over about ten years.

items.prompt: Before the name 'La Niña' caught on, what was another name for this cold phase?

options.label: Super El Niño
Anti-El Niño
El Niño Grande
Pacific Winter

items.explain: In the past, La Niña was also called an anti-El Niño, as well as El Viejo, 'the old man'.

items.prompt: The tropical Pacific is in none of its warm or cold extremes, with no event under way. Which phase of the oscillation is it in?

options.label: La Niña
El Niño
Southern
Neutral

items.explain: The oscillation recurs in three phases: Neutral, La Niña or El Niño, with La Niña and El Niño as the opposite extremes.

items.prompt: Which group would a strong La Niña and the wider cycle it belongs to likely hurt most?

options.label: Office workers in inland European cities
Miners in landlocked Central Asian states
Bankers in wealthy Atlantic financial hubs
Farmers and fishers in developing Pacific countries

items.explain: The countries most affected by ENSO are developing countries bordering the Pacific that depend on agriculture and fishing.

items.prompt: A farmer asks forecasters for the exact year the next La Niña will arrive. What can they honestly offer?

options.label: An exact year, since it comes every four years
No firm year, as the cycle is irregular and hard to predict
An exact year, since it always follows El Niño
Nothing at all, since nobody tracks it

items.explain: The switching between phases is irregular, cycling roughly every two to seven years, and is not easily predictable, though it is closely monitored.
